title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: A Partial History of Action Figures
summary: Rerun of a classic Stuff You Should Know episode, introduced by Josh as part of a "Twelve Days of Christmas Toys" playlist, covering the history of action figures. The hosts trace the lineage from Barbie and Ruth Handler, through Stan Weston's idea and Hasbro's G.I. Joe (1964), to the 1970s Mego superhero and Planet of the Apes lines, Mego's failure to license Star Wars (which went to Kenner), the 1970s-80s shift to smaller 3¾-inch figures, and the G.I. Joe cartoon. They discuss how the FTC's proposed children's advertising restrictions were blocked under Reagan, including his 1988 veto, and how toy-cartoon tie-ins followed. The episode also covers how action figures are sculpted, molded (rotational vs. injection), assembled, and packaged, plus rare and valuable Star Wars figures (Yak Face, Bossk/Weequay-type guards, the Boba Fett missile-shooter, double telescoping lightsabers). It closes with a Kiva microlending listener mail and a plug for the team.
rerun_of: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: A Partial History of Action Figures

segments.title: Rerun introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a classic pick for the Twelve Days of Christmas Toys playlist and invites listeners to weigh in on big vs. small G.I. Joe.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and joke about its title, and mention that the Barbie episode is a favorite and Barbie figures into this one.

segments.title: Barbie and the search for a boys' doll
segments.summary: Chuck explains that Ruth Handler's Barbie at Mattel was a hit because of its accessories, and toy companies wanted a similar model for boys, which required a boy's doll concept.

segments.title: Stan Weston and the soldier doll idea
segments.summary: Stan Weston, a military history buff in the toy business, pitched a soldier doll series to Hasbro VP Don Levine in 1963, who suggested the name action figures. Stan reportedly received $100,000, about $782,000 in today's money.

segments.title: G.I. Joe's 1964 debut and the four original figures
segments.summary: G.I. Joe debuted in 1964 as a twelve-inch figure with about twenty-one moving parts. G.I. Joe was the collective name for Armed Forces figures Rocky (Army), Skip (Navy), and Ace (Air Force), who were largely identical apart from clothing. The hosts recall differing face details and the scar and inverted thumbnail flaws.

segments.title: Innovations: articulation, packaging, and knockoffs
segments.summary: Chuck notes the figure's articulation and kung fu grip (added mid-1970s), the 'collect them all' packaging that showed other figures, and that Hasbro released cheap Defenders knockoffs in the seventies. Josh cites that G.I. Joe made about 66 percent of Hasbro's profits in 1964.

segments.title: G.I. Joe accessories and the adventurer rebrand
segments.summary: The hosts discuss accessories such as Josh's jet pack and submarine. G.I. Joe sales fell during the Vietnam War, so the line was pulled and rebranded as adventurers, with a name taken from the 1945 film The Story of G.I. Joe.
topics: Vietnam War impact on toy sales

segments.title: Gap left by G.I. Joe and transition to Mego
segments.summary: With G.I. Joe off the market, a void opened that Mego filled. The segment leads into a break.

segments.title: Mego pronunciation and the superhero line
segments.summary: The hosts debate how to say Mego. Chuck explains that Mego, around 1971 or 1972, launched the World's Greatest Superheroes line of eight-inch figures, which was a big hit.

segments.title: Mego's licensed characters and playsets
segments.summary: Mego licensed famous characters from Marvel and DC, including Spider-Man, Hulk, Batman, Wonder Woman, Iron Man and Captain America, and produced villains, side characters, the Batmobile and Batcave playset. It also sold non-superhero alter egos exclusively through Montgomery Ward, and launched a Planet of the Apes line in 1973.

segments.title: Mego's Star Trek line and the Star Wars license mistake
segments.summary: Mego's Star Trek line included playsets, and the hosts note the figures shrank from twelve to eight inches. Mego declined the Star Wars license, which went to Kenner. Two accounts exist, with the more plausible being a decision not to invest, and the second, about contract signers being out of town, sourced to a single blog.

segments.title: Shrinking figures: from G.I. Joe to Microman
segments.summary: G.I. Joe licensed overseas: Action Man in the UK and Takara in Japan. After the 1970s oil crisis, smaller figures were developed, with Microman released in 1974, leading to the three-and-three-quarter-inch scale.

segments.title: Big vs. small G.I. Joe debate
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh argue about whether the twelve-inch or the three-and-three-quarter-inch G.I. Joe is superior. Chuck prefers the small ones and Josh the big ones.

segments.title: G.I. Joe cartoon and the Cobra storyline
segments.summary: The G.I. Joe cartoon in the early eighties gave characters names and backstories and set G.I. Joe against Cobra, led by Cobra Commander and villains including Serpentor, Tomax and Xamot. Chuck says the cartoon made the characters' stories central to play.

segments.title: FTC children's advertising rules and the Reagan veto
segments.summary: In the late 1970s the FTC studied regulating marketing to children and found young children could not distinguish ads from programs. Business lobbied against it, and in 1980 Reagan appointed an FTC chairman favoring deregulation. Warlike toys and cartoons returned. In November 1988 Reagan vetoed a children's programming bill that had passed Congress, which would have limited advertising time and required educational programs. Toy companies and broadcasters also made deals linking cartoons to toy sales.

segments.title: Cartoon quality debate and marketing to kids
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether deregulation hurt cartoon creativity. Chuck says G.I. Joe had overarching storylines, unlike older cartoons, and the hosts agree to do a future episode on marketing to kids.

segments.title: Kenner's Star Wars figures and sales
segments.summary: Chuck says Kenner launched the three-and-three-quarter-inch Star Wars line in 1978, selling about forty million units a year and about three hundred million overall through 1985. Josh recalls his own collection and not realizing collectibility as a kid.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break between segments.

segments.title: Action figure history wrap-up and toy-collectible trends
segments.summary: Josh covers the later growth of action figures from Transformers and Marvel and DC toys, to movie and TV tie-ins like a Scarface figure. Chuck notes that companies sometimes release limited variants, such as figures missing a thumb, to create collector value, which Josh questions.

segments.title: How action figures are designed and sculpted
segments.summary: A sculptor builds an armature, sculpts clay around it, and works on separate parts like the head and arms, sometimes carving clothing. The hosts note that making a figure takes about two weeks and that the materials include ABS plastic and polypropylene or polyethylene.

segments.title: Molding: rotational vs. injection molding
segments.summary: Making molds takes about two-thirds of the time. Rotational molding gives smooth figures with less detail, while injection molding keeps detail but can leave seams. Star Wars figures were noted for seams and detail limits, and Chuck argues the small figures were made to be played with.

segments.title: Assembly, packaging, and collecting cards
segments.summary: Figures are assembled and painted, then placed in cardboard-backed clear plastic packaging. G.I. Joe packages later included backstory cards. The hosts discuss old trading cards and that most of the manufacturing happens overseas.

segments.title: Rare and valuable Star Wars figures
segments.summary: The hosts discuss rare Star Wars figures: Yak Face, a Jabba the Hut guard from the Power of the Force line and a rare figure sent to Europe; Weequay, with a special freeze-frame variant; the vinyl-caped Jawa; and the Boba Fett figure that fired a missile, which was pulled over choking-hazard concerns. Sales figures range widely.

segments.title: Double telescoping lightsabers and unresolved questions
segments.summary: Josh describes double telescoping lightsabers for Obi-Wan, Darth Vader and Luke as very rare and valuable. The hosts note they have seen conflicting claims about the 'holy grail' figure and call for expert clarification.

segments.title: Fan resource shout-outs
segments.summary: Chuck recommends the Yojoe.com fan site, his gallery of knockoff toys, and the G.I. Joe PSAs by Eric Fenzler.

segments.title: Closing remarks
segments.summary: Chuck closes the episode and suggests searching for action figures online for more information.

segments.title: Listener mail and Kiva microlending plug
segments.summary: The hosts read a listener email from Jordan about Kiva microlending and promote the Stuff You Should Know Kiva team, which has over nine thousand members and nearly four million dollars in loans.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Kiva team

segments.title: Contact information and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives social media and email contact details for the show and the outro plays.
